newsitem.title: CHINA: China copper needs confused - traders.
newsitem.headline: China copper needs confused - traders.

text.p: China's lack of activity on the international copper market is confounding metals traders worldwide, with little consistency in views on when, or even if, Chinese buying will begin.
Some traders polled in recent days said China has enough stock to keep its industry going for most of 1997.
Others said China must buy, and buy soon, and that when it does the quantities will be huge and the effect on the world price significant.
Chinese trading sources said there is no money to buy. Even if there was, current prices are too high.
Copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) has been consolidating for the past couple of weeks below $2,400 a tonne. On Tuesday, three months copper closed unchanged at $2,360.
China's official press said earlier this year that 170,000 tonnes of copper left over from imports in 1996 will keep the market happy this year.

A producer source said 170,000 tonnes accounted for 15 to 17 percent of annual demand of and should have run out by now given healthy demand for copper products as construction and infrastructure projects continue apace.
State Statistical Bureau figures show China's copper output in the first two months of 1997 up almost 12 percent on the same period of 1996, at 145,900 tonnes.
The head of research at Brandeis (Brokers) Limited, Robin Bhar, said up to 100,000 tonnes of copper had been imported by China since September 1996.
Some of this was for consumption, some for the government's strategic stockpile and some for arbitrage trading, he said.

Bhar told Reuters in Shanghai that Chinese customs figures on 1996 imports could be out by 100,000 to 150,000 tonnes and that 1996 net refined copper imports could be closer to 300,000 tonnes than the official 150,000 tonnes.
This discrepancy, he said, resulted from the fact that the flow of copper between bonded warehouses and the Western market is not included in official import figures.
And it could mean that China has the copper to sell back onto the market, which would push prices down -- and make them more attractive for the price-conscious Chinese.
Traders also suggested the State Reserve Bureau could be lending copper to end-users while it waits for prices to fall.
Traders said Chinese copper was being offered last week at the LME cash price plus a premium of $20-30 a tonne, pushing premiums down from around $100.
With no takers even at that price, that copper could now be offered to domestic users, adding to internal supply and keeping China off the market longer, some traders said.

Bankers Trust said on Tuesday China's copper consumption is likely to hit 1.621 million tonnes in 1997, rising to 1.862 million in 1998 and pushing the market to a deficit this year of 210,000 tonnes, and next year of 472,000 tonnes.
China's 1997 copper demand has been officially put at 1.2 million tonnes.

In a report released in London, Bankers Trust said China's metal demand in recent years has probably been greatly underestimated because of the difficulty of tracking an economy that has been growing at around 10 percent a year for 15 years.
A producer source in Asia said China's copper demand should be outstripping gross domestic product (GDP).
China's GDP grew at 9.7 percent in 1996 and 9.4 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
